title: 'Excited delirium' blamed
article: --- A coroner's jury has concluded that "excited delirium" -- and not pepper spray -- ultimately resulted in the death of a 32-year-old Regina man who died in a struggle with police and paramedics.

While Vernon Dale Crowe's death sparked controversy about the use of pepper spray by Regina police, a coroner's jury was silent on the tool in its 10 recommendations reached after five hours of deliberations Wednesday.

"At the end this wasn't a case about pepper spray," lawyer Aaron Fox, who represented police officers, told reporters following the inquest. "I think the jury's recommendations reflect that," he said.
But not everyone agrees pepper spray played no role in Crowe's death.
Earlier in the day during a vigil outside the courthouse for her cousin, a tearful Vonda Knipfel said evidence at the inquest suggests pepper spray made Crowe, an epileptic, "more and more agitated."
And it was that agitation or "excited delirium" which caused Crowe's heart to beat so erratically on July 10, 2001 that he died, two pathologists testified.

Crowe family lawyer Darren Winegarden told reporters that the family, who weren't present in the courtroom when the inquest ended just after 10 p.m., will likely be discouraged by the lack of a recommendation on pepper spray.

"I think that it might have been beneficial to note the fact pepper spray isn't appropriate in all situations," he said. Winegarden said one of the family's key concerns was that pepper spray was used in a medical situation.
Crowe died on July 10, 2001 just 20 minutes after climbing into an ambulance to be assessed following an epileptic seizure suffered inside Souls Harbour Mission.

The jury recommended changes in microphones and radios to allow paramedics better communication with the hospital and its dispatch; giving the ambulance service and paramedics remote access to patient history; more training to emergency personnel on excited delirium; better restraints and padding in ambulances; the use of faster acting, safe sedatives by paramedics; the use of medical alert bracelets by epileptics; counselling for caregivers about the side effects of a post-seizure state.

Crowe, a usually "happy-go-lucky" man, initially co-operated with paramedics but started to become agitated about two minutes into his check-up. The inquest heard he suffered from a form of epilepsy that can cause a person to be aggressive following a seizure.

Paramedics struggled with Crowe and ended up placing three calls to police for help. Paramedic Jason Williams said it was never an option just to let Crowe leave because they felt he "didn't have control of his faculties."

Const. Dean Ross handcuffed Crowe in the front, but he continued thrashing about. Ross said he "instinctively" pepper sprayed Crowe when the man unintentionally bit and head-butted the officer. The paramedic injected Crowe with a sedative, but it takes 10 to 12 minutes to take effect.
Three additional paramedics and four police officers arrived. Crowe was placed on his stomach with his hands cuffed behind his head and feet bound. Ten minutes later, he had no pulse.
Winegarden raised questions about whether Crowe was hog-tied which would have further impaired his breathing, but police and paramedics maintained that never occurred.
Pathologist Dr. Lloyd Denmark said Crowe's position and restraints could have also played a role in his death by affecting his breathing.
However, he added that emergency personnel likely had little option given his state. "Unfortunately, you can't help these people unless you restrain them," he testified.
